history.q: Which Danish king boasted on a runestone at Jelling that he "made the Danes Christian"?
history.fact: Harald's great Jelling stone, raised around 965, is often called Denmark's birth certificate.

history.q: Which Danish king ruled England, Denmark and Norway in the early 11th century?
history.fact: Cnut's "North Sea Empire" did not outlast his sons, and his remains lie in Winchester Cathedral in England.

history.q: Which country occupied Denmark from April 1940 to May 1945?
history.fact: The Danish government stayed in office until August 1943, when it resigned rather than accept new German demands.

history.q: Which Danish queen brought Denmark, Norway and Sweden together in the Kalmar Union of 1397?
history.fact: Margaret had her young grand-nephew, Eric of Pomerania, crowned king of all three realms at Kalmar.

history.q: Which British admiral is said to have put a telescope to his blind eye at the Battle of Copenhagen in 1801?
history.fact: According to the story, Nelson pretended not to see his commander's signal to withdraw and fought on.

history.q: Which Caribbean islands, now a US territory, did Denmark sell to the United States in 1917?
history.fact: The United States paid $25 million in gold for St Thomas, St John and St Croix.

history.q: Which country did Denmark have to give up to Sweden in 1814?
history.fact: Under the Treaty of Kiel, Denmark kept Norway's old Atlantic possessions: Greenland, Iceland and the Faroe Islands.

history.q: In October 1943, most of Denmark's Jews escaped Nazi deportation by crossing to which country?
history.fact: Fishermen and ordinary Danes ferried about 7,000 people across the Øresund in small boats.

history.q: Which Danish king built Copenhagen's Round Tower and Rosenborg Castle?
history.fact: Christian IV reigned from 1588 to 1648, the longest reign of any Danish monarch.

history.q: According to legend, the Danish flag fell from the sky during a 1219 battle in which present-day country?
history.fact: The Dannebrog is often cited as the oldest national flag still in continuous use.

history.q: In 1864, Denmark lost Schleswig and Holstein after a war against Prussia and which other power?
history.fact: The defeat at Dybbøl on 18 April 1864 remains a defining moment in Danish national memory.

history.q: After a 1920 plebiscite, which region returned from Germany to Denmark?
history.fact: The border drawn by that vote still stands, with a German minority to its north and a Danish minority to its south.

history.q: Which king, father of Harald Bluetooth, raised the smaller Jelling stone in memory of his wife Thyra?
history.fact: Gorm's inscription calls Thyra "Denmark's adornment", one of the earliest mentions of the name Denmark on Danish soil.

history.q: Which Danish king lost Skåne and other eastern provinces to Sweden in 1658?
history.fact: Frederick III used the crisis that followed to make himself an absolute monarch in 1660.

history.q: Ships paying Denmark's Sound Dues passed beneath which castle at Helsingør?
history.fact: Denmark charged ships sailing through the Øresund from 1429 until 1857, and the dues made the crown rich.

history.q: Which Danish Viking king conquered England in 1013?
history.fact: Sweyn died in early 1014 after only about five weeks as king; his son Cnut later won England back.

history.q: In 1792, Denmark became the first European country to decree a ban on which trade, effective from 1803?
history.fact: Slavery itself continued in the Danish West Indies until 1848, when it was abolished after an uprising.

history.q: Which Danish king rode alone on horseback through occupied Copenhagen as a symbol of national spirit?
history.fact: The popular story that he wore a yellow star in solidarity with Danish Jews is a legend, not fact.

history.q: Denmark's Kongeloven (Royal Law) of 1665 was a written constitution for what kind of rule?
history.fact: It was the only formal constitution of absolutism in Europe, and the king answered to God alone.

history.q: During which king's reign were Denmark's circular Viking ring fortresses, such as Trelleborg, built?
history.fact: Tree-ring dating places the building of Trelleborg around 980.

history.q: Which bishop is credited with founding Copenhagen in 1167?
history.fact: The ruins of Absalon's castle can still be seen beneath Christiansborg Palace.

history.q: Which Danish king was known as the "father-in-law of Europe"?
history.fact: His children included Queen Alexandra of Britain, Empress Maria Feodorovna of Russia and King George I of Greece.

history.q: In which year did Denmark officially adopt the Lutheran Reformation?
history.fact: Christian III seized the Church's lands after winning a civil war known as the Count's Feud.

history.q: Which medieval Danish historian wrote Gesta Danorum, which contains the Amleth story behind Hamlet?
history.fact: Saxo's tale of Amleth reached Shakespeare through later French retellings.

history.q: Which Danish king, nicknamed "Atterdag", reunited the kingdom and seized Visby on Gotland in 1361?
history.fact: His daughter Margaret went on to rule Denmark, Norway and Sweden in the Kalmar Union.

technology.q: In which Danish town was the LEGO company founded?
technology.fact: The name LEGO comes from the Danish words "leg godt", meaning "play well".

technology.q: Which Danish physicist won the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on the structure of atoms?
technology.fact: His son Aage Bohr also won the Nobel Prize in Physics, in 1975.

technology.q: Which Danish astronomer built the observatory of Uraniborg on the island of Hven?
technology.fact: Tycho lost part of his nose in a duel as a student and wore a metal replacement for the rest of his life.

technology.q: Which Danish brewery, founded in 1847, is known for the slogan "Probably the best beer in the world"?
technology.fact: Founder J.C. Jacobsen named it after his son Carl, and its laboratory isolated the first pure lager yeast in 1883.

technology.q: Which Danish shipping giant uses a white seven-pointed star on a blue background as its logo?
technology.fact: The company was founded in 1904 by Peter Mærsk Møller and his son A.P. Møller.

technology.q: Which Danish drugmaker makes Ozempic and Wegovy?
technology.fact: Its roots go back to 1923, when Nordisk began making insulin just after the hormone was discovered.

technology.q: Which Danish company is one of the world's biggest makers of wind turbines?
technology.fact: Vestas started as a blacksmith's shop in 1898 and built its first wind turbines in 1979.

technology.q: Which Danish physicist discovered in 1820 that an electric current can move a compass needle?
technology.fact: Ørsted's discovery linked electricity and magnetism, and in 1825 he also produced aluminium.

technology.q: Which Danish audio and TV brand is famous for its sleek modernist design?
technology.fact: Peter Bang and Svend Olufsen founded the company in 1925 in Struer, in western Jutland.

technology.q: Which Danish astronomer first showed that light has a finite speed, in 1676?
technology.fact: Rømer timed the eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io and noticed they ran late when Jupiter was farther from Earth.

technology.q: Which Danish company's name combines "ventilation" and "lux", the Latin for light?
technology.fact: Engineer Villum Kann Rasmussen founded the roof-window maker in 1941.

technology.q: What did Danish engineer Valdemar Poulsen's 1898 "telegraphone" pioneer?
technology.fact: It recorded on steel wire; a recording of Emperor Franz Joseph made in 1900 is among the oldest surviving magnetic recordings.

technology.q: Danish computer scientist Bjarne Stroustrup created which programming language?
technology.fact: He began the work at Bell Labs in 1979, when the language was called "C with Classes".

technology.q: Greenland-born Danish-Canadian programmer Rasmus Lerdorf created which web language?
technology.fact: PHP originally stood for "Personal Home Page".

technology.q: The world's first offshore wind farm was built in 1991 off which Danish island?
technology.fact: The Vindeby farm's 11 turbines generated power for about 25 years before being taken down in 2017.

technology.q: Which interpretation of quantum mechanics is named after the city where Niels Bohr worked?
technology.fact: Bohr's institute in Copenhagen, opened in 1921, drew young physicists such as Werner Heisenberg and Wolfgang Pauli.

technology.q: Which Danish chemist introduced the pH scale in 1909?
technology.fact: He developed it at the Carlsberg Laboratory while studying the chemistry of proteins and brewing.

technology.q: Danish physician Niels Finsen won the 1903 Nobel Prize for treating disease with what?
technology.fact: Finsen used concentrated light to treat lupus vulgaris, a disfiguring skin form of tuberculosis.

technology.q: Which Danish company, founded in 1945 in Bjerringbro, is one of the world's largest pump makers?
technology.fact: Founder Poul Due Jensen started by building water pumps for farms in Jutland.

technology.q: Danish engineer Anders Hejlsberg was the lead architect of which Microsoft programming language?
technology.fact: He had earlier written Turbo Pascal and later co-designed TypeScript.

technology.q: Which Danish scientist won the 1920 Nobel Prize for discovering how capillaries regulate blood flow in muscles?
technology.fact: After visiting Canada, Krogh helped bring insulin production to Denmark, founding what became part of Novo Nordisk.

technology.q: Which vitamin did Danish biochemist Henrik Dam discover?
technology.fact: The K stands for "koagulation", because the vitamin is needed for blood to clot.

technology.q: Which Danish seismologist discovered in 1936 that the Earth has a solid inner core?
technology.fact: She worked it out from seismic waves of a 1929 New Zealand earthquake, and lived to the age of 104.

technology.q: Which engineering company did Mads Clausen found in his parents' farmhouse on the island of Als in 1933?
technology.fact: Danfoss, best known for valves, thermostats and drives, still has its headquarters at Nordborg on Als.

technology.q: Whose early temperature scale influenced Daniel Fahrenheit, who visited him in Copenhagen in 1708?
technology.fact: On Rømer's scale, water froze at 7.5 degrees and boiled at 60.

art.q: Which Danish author wrote "The Little Mermaid" and "The Ugly Duckling"?
art.fact: Andersen's fairy tales have been translated into more than 125 languages.

art.q: Which Danish architect designed the Sydney Opera House?
art.fact: Utzon left the project in 1966 and never saw the finished building in person.

art.q: Shakespeare's Hamlet is set at Elsinore, the castle known in Danish as what?
art.fact: Hamlet is often staged in the castle's courtyard; Laurence Olivier played the prince there in 1937.

art.q: Which Danish philosopher is often called the father of existentialism?
art.fact: Kierkegaard published many books under pseudonyms, including Either/Or (1843), signed "Victor Eremita".

art.q: Which Danish author wrote the memoir Out of Africa?
art.fact: She often wrote in English as Isak Dinesen, and her former farmhouse near Nairobi is now a museum.

art.q: Which Danish director made Breaking the Waves and Dancer in the Dark?
art.fact: Dancer in the Dark, starring Björk, won the Palme d'Or at Cannes in 2000.

art.q: Which Danish actor played the Bond villain Le Chiffre in Casino Royale (2006)?
art.fact: Mikkelsen won Best Actor at Cannes in 2012 for the Danish drama The Hunt.

art.q: Which Danish-Norwegian pop group had a worldwide hit with "Barbie Girl" in 1997?
art.fact: Toy maker Mattel sued the band's record label over the song and lost.

art.q: Which Danish designer created the Egg and Swan chairs?
art.fact: He designed them for Copenhagen's SAS Royal Hotel, where he designed everything down to the cutlery.

art.q: Which Danish furniture designer created the Wishbone Chair?
art.fact: Wegner designed more than 500 chairs during his career.

art.q: Which Danish designer created the PH Artichoke lamp?
art.fact: Henningsen's layered shades were designed to give soft light without any glare from the bulb.

art.q: Which artists' colony gathered at a fishing village on Denmark's northern tip in the late 1800s?
art.fact: P.S. Krøyer's beach scenes captured the famous soft light of Skagen's summer evenings.

art.q: Which Danish painter is known for quiet grey interiors, often with a woman seen from behind?
art.fact: Many of his interiors show his own Copenhagen apartment at Strandgade 30.

art.q: Which Danish composer wrote six symphonies, including "The Inextinguishable"?
art.fact: Nielsen grew up on the island of Funen, and his portrait appeared on the 100-krone banknote.

art.q: Which Danish architect designed CopenHill, a waste-to-energy plant with a ski slope on its roof?
art.fact: The plant, opened in 2019, burns city waste to make electricity and heat for Copenhagen homes.

art.q: The Danish TV drama Borgen follows a woman who becomes what?
art.fact: "Borgen" ("The Castle") is the nickname for Christiansborg Palace, home of the Danish parliament.

art.q: Which Danish film, based on a Karen Blixen story, won the 1988 Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film?
art.fact: Bille August's Pelle the Conqueror won the same award a year later.

art.q: Which Danish-Icelandic artist installed a giant artificial sun in Tate Modern's Turbine Hall in 2003?
art.fact: The Weather Project drew about two million visitors, many of whom lay on the floor to gaze at the mirrored ceiling.

art.q: Which painter is called the father of Danish painting and led its Golden Age?
art.fact: Eckersberg studied in Paris under Jacques-Louis David before teaching a generation of Danish artists.

art.q: Which Danish neoclassical sculptor has a museum dedicated to his work beside Christiansborg Palace?
art.fact: Thorvaldsens Museum opened in 1848 as the first purpose-built museum building in Denmark.

art.q: Which Danish painter co-founded the avant-garde CoBrA movement in 1948?
art.fact: CoBrA took its name from the home cities of its founders: Copenhagen, Brussels and Amsterdam.

art.q: Which Danish novelist, author of Lucky Per, shared the 1917 Nobel Prize in Literature?
art.fact: Bille August turned Lucky Per into a film in 2018.

art.q: Which Danish poet structured her book-length poem "alphabet" on the Fibonacci sequence?
art.fact: Each section begins with a new letter, starting with apricot trees, and grows by the Fibonacci numbers.

art.q: Which Danish city's ARoS art museum is crowned by a circular rainbow-coloured walkway?
art.fact: Olafur Eliasson's "Your rainbow panorama" opened on the museum's roof in 2011.

art.q: Which director made Festen (The Celebration), the first film of the Dogme 95 movement?
art.fact: Festen won the Jury Prize at Cannes in 1998.

politics.q: What is the name of Denmark's parliament?
politics.fact: Its 179 members include two elected in Greenland and two in the Faroe Islands.

politics.q: Which Copenhagen palace houses the Danish parliament, the Prime Minister's Office and the Supreme Court?
politics.fact: The palace stands on Slotsholmen, the islet where Bishop Absalon built Copenhagen's first castle.

politics.q: Which queen reigned over Denmark from 1972 to 2024?
politics.fact: A talented artist, she designed theatre costumes and illustrated a Danish edition of The Lord of the Rings.

politics.q: In which year did Denmark join the European Economic Community, forerunner of the EU?
politics.fact: Denmark joined on the same day as the United Kingdom and Ireland.

politics.q: Which currency did Danish voters reject in a 2000 referendum?
politics.fact: Denmark kept the krone, but keeps it tightly pegged to the euro.

politics.q: Denmark was a founding member of which alliance in 1949?
politics.fact: The wartime occupation convinced Denmark to give up its long-standing policy of neutrality.

politics.q: Which Copenhagen palace complex is the main residence of the Danish royal family?
politics.fact: It consists of four identical rococo palaces arranged around an octagonal square.

politics.q: Which self-governing territory in the Danish Realm is the world's largest island?
politics.fact: Greenland's 2009 Self-Government Act recognised Greenlanders as a people under international law.

politics.q: Denmark regularly tops Transparency International's global index for what?
politics.fact: Denmark has ranked first, sometimes jointly, in most recent editions of the Corruption Perceptions Index.

politics.q: On which date does Denmark celebrate Constitution Day?
politics.fact: On 5 June 1849, King Frederick VII signed the constitution that ended absolute monarchy.

politics.q: Who became Denmark's first female prime minister in 2011?
politics.fact: After leaving office she became chief executive of Save the Children International.

politics.q: Which Danish politician served as the EU's competition commissioner from 2014 to 2024?
politics.fact: Vestager became known worldwide for her cases against tech giants such as Google and Apple.

politics.q: Which former Danish prime minister became NATO Secretary General in 2009?
politics.fact: He had led Denmark's government from 2001 to 2009 and headed NATO until 2014.

politics.q: In 1992, Danish voters rejected which EU treaty before approving it with opt-outs a year later?
politics.fact: The 1993 deal let Denmark stay out of the euro and parts of EU defence, justice and citizenship cooperation.

politics.q: What is Denmark's labour-market model, combining easy hiring and firing with strong unemployment support, called?
politics.fact: The model relies on generous unemployment benefits and active retraining to help people back into work.

politics.q: In 1953, Denmark abolished which chamber, making its parliament unicameral?
politics.fact: The same 1953 reforms also allowed a woman to inherit the Danish throne.

politics.q: Which Social Democrat led Denmark's government from 1929 to 1942?
politics.fact: Stauning's 1933 Kanslergade Agreement is often seen as a foundation stone of the Danish welfare state.

politics.q: Which Conservative led Denmark's centre-right governments from 1982 to 1993?
politics.fact: He was the first leader of the Conservative People's Party to become prime minister.

politics.q: In which year did Danish women win the right to vote in national elections?
politics.fact: The constitutional amendment was signed on 5 June 1915, Constitution Day.

politics.q: What share of the national vote does a party need to win seats in the Folketing?
politics.fact: The low threshold means Danish parliaments often include ten or more parties.

politics.q: What is the name of the Danish prime minister's official residence, north of Copenhagen?
politics.fact: The manor house in Kongens Lyngby has been used by prime ministers since the 1960s.

politics.q: Which king signed Denmark's first democratic constitution in 1849?
politics.fact: Frederick VII died without children in 1863, ending the main line of the House of Oldenburg.

politics.q: Under the Danish constitution, what share of Folketing members can demand a referendum on a passed bill?
politics.fact: The rule has been used only once, in 1963, when voters rejected a package of land laws.

politics.q: Besides Denmark and Greenland, which territory forms the Danish Realm?
politics.fact: The Faroe Islands have had home rule since 1948 and have their own parliament, the Løgting.

politics.q: Who led the Danish People's Party from its founding in 1995 until 2012?
politics.fact: She later served as Speaker of the Folketing from 2015 to 2019.

current-affairs.q: Who became King of Denmark on 14 January 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Queen Margrethe II announced her abdication in her New Year's Eve speech, after 52 years on the throne.

current-affairs.q: In April 2024, fire destroyed the dragon-tail spire of which historic Copenhagen building?
current-affairs.fact: As the 17th-century building burned, staff and passers-by carried priceless paintings out to safety.

current-affairs.q: Which Danish film won the Oscar for Best International Feature Film in April 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Director Thomas Vinterberg dedicated the film to his daughter Ida, who died in an accident early in filming.

current-affairs.q: Who became Denmark's youngest-ever prime minister in June 2019?
current-affairs.fact: The Social Democrat leader was 41 when she took office.

current-affairs.q: In August 2019, US President Donald Trump publicly floated buying which territory of the Danish Realm?
current-affairs.fact: Denmark's prime minister called the idea absurd, and Trump postponed a planned state visit to Copenhagen.

current-affairs.q: In January 2025, Denmark's men won a record fourth world title in a row in which sport?
current-affairs.fact: Their run of titles began in 2019, and they also won Olympic handball gold in Paris in 2024.

current-affairs.q: Which Danish cyclist won the Tour de France in both 2022 and 2023?
current-affairs.fact: Vingegaard also finished second to Tadej Pogačar in 2021 and 2024.

current-affairs.q: Which Danish city hosted the Grand Départ, the opening stages, of the 2022 Tour de France?
current-affairs.fact: It was the northernmost start in the race's history.

current-affairs.q: In August 2024, Viktor Axelsen won a second Olympic gold medal in which sport?
current-affairs.fact: He became the first man to defend the Olympic singles title since China's Lin Dan.

current-affairs.q: In September 2023, which Danish drugmaker overtook LVMH as Europe's most valuable listed company?
current-affairs.fact: Demand for its weight-loss drug Wegovy pushed its stock market value past the size of Denmark's entire economy.

current-affairs.q: Which Danish footballer suffered a cardiac arrest on the pitch during Euro 2020 in June 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Teammates shielded him as medics restarted his heart, and he returned to international football in 2022.

current-affairs.q: In a June 2022 referendum, Danish voters chose to drop their EU opt-out in which area?
current-affairs.fact: About two-thirds voted yes, three months after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

current-affairs.q: Which party, founded by former prime minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen, entered government in December 2022?
current-affairs.fact: It joined the Social Democrats and Venstre in a rare government spanning the left-right divide.

current-affairs.q: In 2023, Denmark's parliament voted to abolish which public holiday to help fund defence spending?
current-affairs.fact: Great Prayer Day, introduced in 1686, became an ordinary working day from 2024.

current-affairs.q: Which Danish chemist shared the 2022 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing click chemistry?
current-affairs.fact: He shared the prize with Americans Carolyn Bertozzi and K. Barry Sharpless.

current-affairs.q: In November 2020, Denmark ordered a cull of all farmed animals of which species over a coronavirus mutation?
current-affairs.fact: The order covered roughly 15 million animals and was later found to have lacked a clear legal basis.

current-affairs.q: In August 2023, Denmark and the Netherlands pledged which fighter jets to Ukraine?
current-affairs.fact: The Royal Danish Air Force had flown F-16s since 1980.

current-affairs.q: In November 2022, which 19-year-old Dane beat Novak Djokovic to win the Paris Masters?
current-affairs.fact: It was Rune's first Masters 1000 title, and it carried him into the world's top ten.

current-affairs.q: Which party finished second in the vote at Denmark's November 2022 general election?
current-affairs.fact: The Social Democrats came first with 27.5%, their best result in over two decades.

current-affairs.q: Which party, founded by Inger Støjberg in 2022, won 14 seats at its first general election?
current-affairs.fact: Støjberg had previously served as a Venstre minister.

current-affairs.q: Which title did UNESCO and the International Union of Architects give Copenhagen for 2023?
current-affairs.fact: Copenhagen also hosted the UIA World Congress of Architects that July.

current-affairs.q: In December 2020, Denmark's parliament voted to end all oil and gas extraction in its North Sea by which year?
current-affairs.fact: Denmark, then the EU's largest oil producer, also cancelled all future licensing rounds.

current-affairs.q: In 2024, construction was under way on the Fehmarn Belt tunnel linking Lolland with which German island?
current-affairs.fact: About 18 km long, it is set to be the world's longest immersed road and rail tunnel.

current-affairs.q: How far did Denmark's men's team go at the Euro 2020 football championship, played in 2021?
current-affairs.fact: They lost 2-1 to England after extra time at Wembley.

current-affairs.q: In 2022, Queen Margrethe II announced that the children of which son would lose their prince and princess titles?
current-affairs.fact: From 1 January 2023, Joachim's four children became counts and countess of Monpezat.

general.q: What is the capital of Denmark?
general.fact: Its Danish name, København, means "merchants' harbour".

general.q: Which Danish word describes a cosy, contented, candlelit atmosphere?
general.fact: Hygge was shortlisted for the Oxford Dictionaries Word of the Year in 2016.

general.q: Which amusement park opened in the centre of Copenhagen in 1843?
general.fact: Walt Disney visited Tivoli and is said to have drawn inspiration from it for Disneyland.

general.q: Which famous bronze statue sits on a rock by Copenhagen's Langelinie promenade?
general.fact: Sculpted by Edvard Eriksen and unveiled in 1913, she is only about 1.25 m tall.

general.q: What are Danish open sandwiches on rye bread called?
general.fact: The base is usually dense rye bread, rugbrød, topped with anything from herring to roast beef.

general.q: What is the name of the peninsula that forms mainland Denmark?
general.fact: Denmark also has more than 400 named islands, about 70 of them inhabited.

general.q: In 1992, Denmark won which football tournament after being called up as a late replacement?
general.fact: Denmark replaced Yugoslavia about ten days before kick-off and beat Germany 2-0 in the final.

general.q: Which is the only country that shares a land border with Denmark?
general.fact: The border runs across southern Jutland for about 68 km.

general.q: Copenhagen is world-famous for which way of getting around?
general.fact: Some of its busy routes have traffic lights timed to give cyclists a "green wave".

general.q: What do Danes call the pastries known abroad as "Danishes"?
general.fact: The name means "Viennese bread"; Austrian bakers hired during a bakers' strike in the 1850s are said to have brought the technique.

general.q: Roughly how high is Denmark's highest natural point?
general.fact: The summit, Møllehøj near Skanderborg in Jutland, rises just 170.86 m above sea level.

general.q: Which fixed link connects the islands of Funen and Zealand?
general.fact: Its East Bridge has a main span of 1,624 m, one of the longest suspension spans in the world.

general.q: In which Danish city was Hans Christian Andersen born?
general.fact: Odense's H.C. Andersen museum, redesigned by Japanese architect Kengo Kuma, reopened in 2021.

general.q: Which town, founded in the early 700s, is generally considered Denmark's oldest?
general.fact: Ribe began as a Viking-age trading place on the edge of the Wadden Sea marshes.

general.q: In which cathedral are most of Denmark's kings and queens buried?
general.fact: Around 40 Danish monarchs rest in this brick cathedral, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

general.q: Which round Danish Christmas treats are cooked in a special dimpled pan?
general.fact: The name means "apple slices", but they usually contain no apple and are dusted with sugar and dipped in jam.

general.q: Roskilde Festival, first held in 1971, is best known as what?
choices: One of Europe's biggest music festivals
general.fact: The festival is run as a non-profit, and its proceeds go to charity and cultural causes.

general.q: At Grenen, near Skagen at Denmark's northern tip, which two seas meet?
choices: The North Sea and the Baltic
The Wadden Sea and the North Sea
general.fact: Visitors can stand with one foot in each sea as the waves clash over the sandbar.

general.q: In which Copenhagen district did settlers found the self-proclaimed "Freetown Christiania" in 1971?
general.fact: The community grew up in a former military barracks that squatters occupied.

general.q: Råbjerg Mile, in north Jutland, is famous as what?
general.fact: Pushed by the wind, the huge dune creeps north-east by about 15 m a year.

general.q: Which UNESCO-listed tidal flats stretch along Denmark's south-west coast?
general.fact: In spring and autumn, vast flocks of starlings swirl over the marshes in a spectacle called "black sun".

general.q: Which long Danish fjord cuts right across northern Jutland from the Kattegat to the North Sea?
general.fact: A storm broke through to the North Sea in 1825, leaving the land to its north technically an island.

general.q: Which white chalk cliffs on an island south of Zealand rise about 128 m above the Baltic?
general.fact: The chalk formed from the shells of countless tiny sea creatures some 70 million years ago.

general.q: Which dish was voted Denmark's national dish in a 2014 poll?
general.fact: The winner, stegt flæsk med persillesovs, is served with boiled potatoes.

general.q: Which Danish goalkeeper captained Manchester United to Champions League victory in 1999?
general.fact: His son Kasper later became Denmark's goalkeeper too.
